"Ah," said I weakly, "I suppose it is because he does it for a living. Now I …" "Now, you," interrupted the other, "do it for a living, too, because you want your fruit trees to bear fruit, and your roses to thrive, and your cabbages to prosper. Who more merciless than you on slugs and other pests that fly or crawl? No, no, we are all out for a living, you as much as the spider, the spider as much as the fly." "We are all Huns," said I. "What a detestable world it is." "Not at all," said he. "It's a very jolly world. I drink to the health of the spider."

"And you have no pity for the fly?" I said. "Not a little bit." he replied. "I am on the side of right." "Whose side is that?" I asked. "Mine," said he. "We must all act according to our point of view. That's what the greenfly does. That's what the spider does. We shall never in this world get all the points of view in accord. We shall go on scrambling for a living to the end. Sometimes the greenfly will be on top, sometimes the spider. Look at that cherry-tree in the orchard. A month ago its branches were laden with fruit. Now there is not a cherry to be seen. The blackbirds and the starlings have stripped the tree as clean as a bone. Their point of view is that the cherries are provided for them, and they are right. They know nothing of the laws of property which man makes for his own protection. It's no use going out to them and asking them to look at your title-deeds, and reminding them of the policeman and the laws against larceny. Our moral code is for us, not for them.

"We are all creatures of our own point of view," he went on. "Before Jones next door bought a motor-car he had very bitter feelings about motorists—used to call them road-hogs, said he would tax these 'land-torpedoes' out of existence, and was full of sympathy and pity for the poor children coming from school. Now he drives a car as hard as anybody; blows the hoggiest of horns; and says it's disgraceful the way parents allow their children to play about in the streets. "Ah," I murmured faintly, "I guess it's because he earns his living that way. Now I…" "Now you," he interjected, "do the same, as you wish for your fruit trees to yield fruit, for your roses to flourish, and for your cabbages to thrive. Who could be more ruthless than you when dealing with slugs and other creeping or flying nuisances? No, no, we are all striving to survive—yourself just as much as the spider, and the spider just as much as the fly." "We are all Huns," I lamented. "What a loathsome world it is." "Not at all," he countered. "It’s quite a cheerful world, in fact. I raise my glass to the health of the spider."

"And you feel no compassion for the fly?" I queried. "Not in the slightest," he answered. "I stand firmly for what is right." "Whose version of right is that?" I pressed. "Mine," he declared. "Each of us must act based on our own perspective. That’s the nature of the greenfly, just as it is for the spider. We will never be able to align all viewpoints in this world. The struggle for existence will continue indefinitely. At times, the greenfly may prevail; at other moments, the spider will. Take a look at that cherry tree in the orchard. Just a month ago, its boughs were heavy with fruit. Now, not a single cherry remains. The blackbirds and starlings have stripped it bare. From their perspective, those cherries exist solely for them, and they are justified in their actions. They are unaware of the property laws created by humans for their own security. Attempting to show them your title-deeds or remind them of law enforcement and theft regulations is futile. Our moral framework is designed for us alone, not for them.

"We are all products of our unique viewpoints," he continued. "Consider Jones from next door; before he purchased a car, he harbored intense disdain for drivers—he referred to them as road-hogs, advocated for taxing these ‘land-torpedoes’ out of existence, and expressed deep concern for children coming home from school. Now, he drives as aggressively as anyone else; he toots the loudest horn and complains about how parents let their children play in the streets. The only change is his perspective.
